title: Posterior sampling by source-space MCMC via prior-based few-step transport maps

paper.title: Posterior sampling by source-space MCMC via prior-based few-step transport maps
paper.abstract: Abstract Bayesian inference increasingly uses informative but implicit priors represented only by samples, such as historical ensembles, simulator outputs, and pretrained generative models. The same computational problem appears in the test-time guidance task (generalized Bayes), where an explicit positive weight, e.g., an exponentiated reward, tilts an implicit prior. We develop a framework for source-space generalized Bayesian inference that combines inexpensive few-step prior transports with posterior stability guarantees. Specifically, we represent the prior using a one- or few-step improved MeanFlow (iMF) map and perform posterior sampling in its Gaussian source space. We establish Wasserstein error bounds between the exact and learned posteriors in terms of the joint population iMF and auxiliary-velocity loss, decomposed into training suboptimality and model-class approximation error. In the iMF source space, we adopt parallel tempering with preconditioned Crank–Nicolson updates and introduce a hybrid variant that incorporates split Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to improve sampling efficiency. Synthetic experiments show that the proposed framework can approximate posterior distributions accurately and efficiently, while CLIP-guided ImageNet experiments demonstrate its ability to steer a pretrained iMF image prior toward text-specified preferences.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Bayesian inference combines prior knowledge with observations to characterize uncertainty about unknown quantities ( Stuart, 2010 ) . In many applications, however, prior information is available through samples, e.g., historical ensembles, simulator outputs, or pretrained generative models rather than an explicit density ( Patel and Oberai, 2019 ; Chung et al., 2023 ; Lunz et al., 2018 ) . Such prior samples can represent complex structures that are difficult to encode analytically, but their densities and scores are not directly available for posterior Markov chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC). Formally, let x ∈ ℝ d x x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} be an unknown with prior π 0 \pi_{0} available only through i.i.d. samples, and let y y denote observations or a task specification. An approach is to learn the data-space prior score by denoising score matching (DSM) ( Vincent, 2011 ) and combine it with the gradient of an analytic log-likelihood or reward to construct Langevin or Hamiltonian dynamics. Flow-based models ( Chen et al., 2018 ) offer an attractive alternative: flow matching learns a time-dependent vector field through a standard regression objective ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) . This provides a scalable approach to learning expressive transport maps for complex and multimodal priors. Under suitable regularity conditions on the vector field, the resulting ODE flow also defines a diffeomorphism between source and data spaces ( Papamakarios et al., 2021 ) . Source-space guidance for flow-matching models has been explored through both optimization and sampling. D-Flow ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ) optimizes the source variable, while Source-Guided Flow Matching (SGFM) ( Wang et al., 2026b ) samples from the source posterior distribution ( 2 ). Source Parallel Tempering (SPT) ( Wang et al., 2026a ) combines local preconditioned Crank-Nicolson (pCN) ( Beskos et al., 2008 ) updates with replica exchanges ( Earl and Deem, 2005 ) across tempered source distributions to address multimodality. These source-space methods are instances of test-time guidance , incorporating user-specified likelihoods or weights during inference. Their connection to the flow matching objective takes S θ S_{	heta} to be the map induced by the exactly integrated learned flow, via Grönwall’s inequality. In practice, however, numerical ODE solvers are employed, introducing an additional discretization error. Under standard regularity and stability assumptions, a numerical ODE solver of order k k has global error O ⁡ ( h k ) O(h^{k}) ( Hairer et al., 1993 ) . The training objective alone does not control this error. Reducing h h requires more integration steps, increasing the cost of source-space MCMC. Minibatch optimal-transport coupling ( Tong et al., 2024 ) , as used by Wang et al. Thus, guarantees for the exactly integrated learned flow do not by themselves establish posterior stability for a fixed few-step implementation. Likewise, Purohit et al. (2025) use few-step consistency models but do not establish how the consistency-distillation training objective controls the resulting posterior error. In this work, we pursue two complementary objectives: making source-space inference computationally efficient through few-step transports and establishing posterior stability guarantees for the implemented maps via the true population training objective. To this end, we use improved MeanFlow (iMF) ( Geng et al., 2026b ) , which learns interval-average velocities without distillation and natively enables one-step or few-step generation without numerical ODE integration. We further explain why the original MeanFlow objective ( Geng et al., 2026a ) does not directly yield the same guarantee, highlighting that native few-step generation alone can fall short of establishing such stability results. Practically, the iMF maps make source-space gradients inexpensive to evaluate when available, allowing MCMC kernels to optionally exploit them to improve mixing.

sections.heading: Contributions
sections.text: We use iMF transport mappings to represent complex priors available only through samples in generalized Bayesian inference settings. Under stated regularity assumptions, we connect population training suboptimality and model-class approximation error for the joint iMF and auxiliary-velocity objective to posterior stability for the implemented one-step or few-step maps. Building on these transports, we adopt SPT with pCN updates ( Wang et al., 2026a ) to facilitate exploration across modes while exploiting the Gaussian reference structure of the high-dimensional source space. When likelihood or reward gradients are available, we additionally introduce Gaussian-reference split HMC ( Beskos et al., 2011 ) at the coldest temperature of SPT to exploit local posterior geometry and potentially improve mixing. Both local kernels preserve the Gaussian reference measure in their reference dynamics, making them natural choices for inference in high-dimensional source spaces. We evaluate the proposed framework on synthetic posterior sampling and CLIP-guided ImageNet generation, demonstrating accurate and efficient posterior approximation in the synthetic settings and the ability to steer a pretrained image prior toward text-specified preferences.

sections.heading: Transport MCMC
sections.text: Transport maps have long been used to improve MCMC by transforming difficult posterior target distributions into coordinates easier for sampling ( Parno and Marzouk, 2018 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . NeuTra HMC learns a variational transport tailored to posterior geometry, with an amortized extension that accommodates different observations within a specified probabilistic model ( Hoffman et al., 2019 ) .

sections.heading: Score-based and diffusion inverse solvers
sections.text: Diffusion-based inverse solvers offer another way to combine a learned sample-only prior with observations, typically by incorporating likelihood information into the reverse generative process. Diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) ( Chung et al., 2023 ) is a prominent example, enabling posterior-oriented sampling. Its approximate guidance, however, does not generally preserve the desired posterior and can introduce systematic bias beyond that arising from prior learning and numerical discretization. Denoising-score MCMC ( Ramzi et al., 2020 ) learns the prior score from samples using denoising score matching ( Vincent, 2011 ) and combines it with an analytically available likelihood score to perform MCMC directly in data space.

sections.heading: Training-time posterior learning.
sections.text: Complementary to test-time guidance, amortized posterior learning trains observation-conditional generators to directly approximate posterior distributions. Neural posterior estimation and related methods learn from simulated parameter-observation pairs, enabling rapid inference for new observations ( Greenberg et al., 2019 ; Radev et al., 2023 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) . The training cost is shared across subsequent inference tasks, but changes to the observation model beyond those covered during training may require retraining or adaptation.

sections.heading: 4.2 CLIP-guided ImageNet generation
sections.text: We evaluate CLIP-guided 256 × 256 256\times 256 class-conditional ImageNet generation: for a fixed ImageNet class (e.g., bald eagle) and text prompt, the goal is to sample images from that class that favor high image-text alignment. We use the cosine similarity from a frozen pretrained CLIP model ( Radford et al., 2021 ) as the guidance reward. Let z ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and let G c ​ ( z ) G_{c}(z) denote a frozen pretrained transport from the Gaussian source distribution to images in class c c . For a text prompt p p , the learned source posterior is ν θ p ​ ( z ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( − 1 2 ​ ‖ z ‖ 2 + τ ​ CLIP ​ ( G c ​ ( z ) , p ) ) \nu^{p}_{\theta}(z)\propto\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{2}\|z\|^{2}+\tau\mathrm{CLIP}(G_{c}(z),p)\right) with τ = 200 \tau=200 .

sections.heading: Comparison
sections.text: We use the pretrained iMF for class-conditional ImageNet generation ( Geng et al., 2026b ) . We compare iMF+SPT+pCN and iMF+SPT+hybrid against their multi-step counterpart SiT+SPT+pCN, where SiT ( Ma et al., 2024 ) is a pretrained class-conditional flow-matching prior integrated using 125 Heun steps. These methods use eight temperature replicas and eight independent ladders. For iMF-based methods, we run 250 adaptation sweeps, 250 burn-in sweeps, and retain 1,000 post-burn-in samples per ladder, yielding 8,000 retained samples per method. SiT+SPT+pCN is extremely slow in this experiment, we evaluate it under a matched per-prompt sampling-time budget equal to the measured hybrid sampling time (more than 10 10 hours), with an additional one-hour allowance for initialization, scoring, and image export. We also include best-of- K K ( Karthik et al., 2023 ) , K = 12 K=12 , as a reward-based selection baseline, retaining the image with the highest CLIP reward among K K learned-prior independent samples. We produce 8,000 8,000 best-of-K images.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Table 2 reports CLIP rewards and sampling costs for two class-prompt pairs, while Figures 2 and 2 show samples ( R R is the reward) from two ladders per method. JPEG compression is for display only and does not affect reported rewards. The two iMF methods achieve comparable rewards and both outperform SiT+SPT+pCN. Their samples more faithfully depict a running golden retriever amid fallen autumn leaves , whereas SiT+SPT+pCN often misses the autumn setting within its sampling budget of 10-11 hours. For the bald eagle prompt, all three methods depict eagles with outstretched wings , but the iMF methods more consistently include snow-capped mountains whereas SiT+SPT+pCN depicts the eagle against the plain blue sky. In these examples, the hybrid sampler offers no clear improvement in reward or sample quality over iMF+SPT+pCN. Finally, best-of- K K achieves the lowest rewards, suggesting guidance is more effective than independent prior draws. The full results are given in Appendix B.3.2 .

sections.text: We develop few-step iMF source-space inference, linking population training suboptimality and approximation error to posterior stability and end-to-end error bounds under stated assumptions. Hybrid SPT improves efficiency on synthetic benchmarks, while one-step iMF reduces CLIP-guided ImageNet sampling costs relative to multi-step SiT. Quantifying how model-class approximation error ϵ app \epsilon_{\mathrm{app}} decreases with capacity while controlling the regularity constants remains open. We did not use generative AI to generate synthetic datasets. The authors reviewed the AI-assisted material, including text, code, and mathematical arguments. We take full responsibility for the final manuscript, its claims, and all accompanying artifacts, including those produced with generative AI assistance.

sections.text: For each scenario, all models are trained on the same fixed dataset of 20,000 prior samples using four-hidden-layer SiLU networks of width 512, with 16,000 optimizer updates at learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} . The iMF model uses raw time inputs ( r , t ) (r,t) and separate average-velocity and auxiliary-velocity heads; FM and diffusion use four Fourier time harmonics. Both iMF and FM use independent data-noise coupling. For iMF, we sample r , t r,t independently from Unif ⁡ [ 0 , 1 ] \mathrm{Unif}[0,1] , and set the auxiliary-loss weight to λ = 1 \lambda=1 . sections.text: The two iMF samplers share a six-step transport with uniformly spaced times, while FM+SPT+pCN uses 100 RK4 steps (400 network evaluations per transport). During 500 adaptation sweeps, proposal parameters are shared across ladders and updated separately at each temperature using the observed acceptance fraction across the ten ladders. (2016) and the general (leapfrog) HMC range 0.6 0.6 - 0.9 0.9 discussed by Betancourt et al. (2014) . The hottest pCN noise scale remains fixed at 0.999 0.999 . The same computational problem appears in the test-time guidance task (generalized Bayes), where an explicit positive weight, e.g., an exponentiated reward, tilts an implicit prior. We develop a framework for source-space generalized Bayesian inference that combines inexpensive few-step prior transports with posterior stability guarantees. Specifically, we represent the prior using a one- or few-step improved MeanFlow (iMF) map and perform posterior sampling in its Gaussian source space. We establish Wasserstein error bounds between the exact and learned posteriors in terms of the joint population iMF and auxiliary-velocity loss, decomposed into training suboptimality and model-class approximation error. In the iMF source space, we adopt parallel tempering with preconditioned Crank–Nicolson updates and introduce a hybrid variant that incorporates split Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to improve sampling efficiency. Synthetic experiments show that the proposed framework can approximate posterior distributions accurately and efficiently, while CLIP-guided ImageNet experiments demonstrate its ability to steer a pretrained iMF image prior toward text-specified preferences. 1 Introduction Bayesian inference combines prior knowledge with observations to characterize uncertainty about unknown quantities ( Stuart, 2010 ) . In many applications, however, prior information is available through samples, e.g., historical ensembles, simulator outputs, or pretrained generative models rather than an explicit density ( Patel and Oberai, 2019 ; Chung et al., 2023 ; Lunz et al., 2018 ) . Such prior samples can represent complex structures that are difficult to encode analytically, but their densities and scores are not directly available for posterior Markov chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC). Formally, let x ∈ ℝ d x x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} be an unknown with prior π 0 \pi_{0} available only through i.i.d. samples, and let y y denote observations or a task specification. An approach is to learn the data-space prior score by denoising score matching (DSM) ( Vincent, 2011 ) and combine it with the gradient of an analytic log-likelihood or reward to construct Langevin or Hamiltonian dynamics. These samplers are typically unadjusted because a learned score alone does not provide the density ratios needed for Metropolis correction. Nevertheless, the likelihood/weight ℓ y ∘ S θ \ell_{y}\circ S_{	heta} may reintroduce curvature, stiffness, anisotropy, or multimodality, particularly when the observation model is highly informative or nonlinear. Early work by Patel et al. (2022) used a Wasserstein GAN to construct S θ S_{	heta} and applied Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) with the No-U-Turn Sampler ( Hoffman et al., 2014 ) to the resulting low-dimensional latent posterior. However, learning S θ S_{	heta} with a WGAN requires solving an adversarial min-max optimization problem, which can be challenging to stabilize. Flow-based models ( Chen et al., 2018 ) offer an attractive alternative: flow matching learns a time-dependent vector field through a standard regression objective ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Tong et al., 2024 ) . This provides a scalable approach to learning expressive transport maps for complex and multimodal priors. Under suitable regularity conditions on the vector field, the resulting ODE flow also defines a diffeomorphism between source and data spaces ( Papamakarios et al., 2021 ) . Source-space guidance for flow-matching models has been explored through both optimization and sampling. D-Flow ( Ben-Hamu et al., 2024 ) optimizes the source variable, while Source-Guided Flow Matching (SGFM) ( Wang et al., 2026b ) samples from the source posterior distribution ( 2 ). Source Parallel Tempering (SPT) ( Wang et al., 2026a ) combines local preconditioned Crank-Nicolson (pCN) ( Beskos et al., 2008 ) updates with replica exchanges ( Earl and Deem, 2005 ) across tempered source distributions to address multimodality. These source-space methods are instances of test-time guidance , incorporating user-specified likelihoods or weights during inference. For methods that represent the prior through a learned transport ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026a ) , a central theoretical question is how prior-learning error controls the discrepancy between the learned posterior ( S θ ) # ​ ν θ y (S_{	heta})_{\#}
u_{	heta}^{y} and the true posterior π y \pi^{y} in ( 1 ). We refer to this as posterior stability . Existing works have tried to address this question, but a gap remains. Wang et al. (2026b) assume a uniform vector-field approximation bound, ‖ v θ ​ ( x , t ) − v ⁡ ( x , t ) ‖ ∞ ≤ ϵ \|v_{	heta}(x,t)-v(x,t)\|_{\infty}\leq\epsilon where v ⁡ ( x , t ) v(x,t) is the true velocity field and v θ ​ ( x , t ) v_{	heta}(x,t) is the learned velocity field. However, the flow-matching objective controls an average squared error rather than a uniform error. Wang et al. (2026a) address this mismatch by establishing posterior stability in terms of the L 2 L^{2} transport-map error, i.e., 𝔼 z ∼ γ ​ ‖ S ⁡ ( z ) − S θ ​ ( z ) ‖ 2 ≤ ϵ 2 \mathbb{E}_{z\sim\gamma}\|S(z)-S_{	heta}(z)\|^{2}\leq\epsilon^{2} , where S S is the exact transport map induced by v ⁡ ( x , t ) v(x,t) . Their connection to the flow matching objective takes S θ S_{	heta} to be the map induced by the exactly integrated learned flow, via Grönwall’s inequality. In practice, however, numerical ODE solvers are employed, introducing an additional discretization error. Under standard regularity and stability assumptions, a numerical ODE solver of order k k has global error O ⁡ ( h k ) O(h^{k}) ( Hairer et al., 1993 ) . The training objective alone does not control this error. Reducing h h requires more integration steps, increasing the cost of source-space MCMC. Minibatch optimal-transport coupling ( Tong et al., 2024 ) , as used by Wang et al. (2026b) , can encourage straighter trajectories and facilitate few-step integration, but does not by itself provide a bound on this numerical error; their theoretical bound likewise concerns the exactly integrated learned flow. Thus, guarantees for the exactly integrated learned flow do not by themselves establish posterior stability for a fixed few-step implementation. Likewise, Purohit et al. (2025) use few-step consistency models but do not establish how the consistency-distillation training objective controls the resulting posterior error. In this work, we pursue two complementary objectives: making source-space inference computationally efficient through few-step transports and establishing posterior stability guarantees for the implemented maps via the true population training objective. To this end, we use improved MeanFlow (iMF) ( Geng et al., 2026b ) , which learns interval-average velocities without distillation and natively enables one-step or few-step generation without numerical ODE integration. We further explain why the original MeanFlow objective ( Geng et al., 2026a ) does not directly yield the same guarantee, highlighting that native few-step generation alone can fall short of establishing such stability results. Practically, the iMF maps make source-space gradients inexpensive to evaluate when available, allowing MCMC kernels to optionally exploit them to improve mixing. Contributions We use iMF transport mappings to represent complex priors available only through samples in generalized Bayesian inference settings. Under stated regularity assumptions, we connect population training suboptimality and model-class approximation error for the joint iMF and auxiliary-velocity objective to posterior stability for the implemented one-step or few-step maps. Building on these transports, we adopt SPT with pCN updates ( Wang et al., 2026a ) to facilitate exploration across modes while exploiting the Gaussian reference structure of the high-dimensional source space. When likelihood or reward gradients are available, we additionally introduce Gaussian-reference split HMC ( Beskos et al., 2011 ) at the coldest temperature of SPT to exploit local posterior geometry and potentially improve mixing. Both local kernels preserve the Gaussian reference measure in their reference dynamics, making them natural choices for inference in high-dimensional source spaces. We evaluate the proposed framework on synthetic posterior sampling and CLIP-guided ImageNet generation, demonstrating accurate and efficient posterior approximation in the synthetic settings and the ability to steer a pretrained image prior toward text-specified preferences. Other related work Transport MCMC Transport maps have long been used to improve MCMC by transforming difficult posterior target distributions into coordinates easier for sampling ( Parno and Marzouk, 2018 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . NeuTra HMC learns a variational transport tailored to posterior geometry, with an amortized extension that accommodates different observations within a specified probabilistic model ( Hoffman et al., 2019 ) . Score-based and diffusion inverse solvers Diffusion-based inverse solvers offer another way to combine a learned sample-only prior with observations, typically by incorporating likelihood information into the reverse generative process. Diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) ( Chung et al., 2023 ) is a prominent example, enabling posterior-oriented sampling. Its approximate guidance, however, does not generally preserve the desired posterior and can introduce systematic bias beyond that arising from prior learning and numerical discretization. Denoising-score MCMC ( Ramzi et al., 2020 ) learns the prior score from samples using denoising score matching ( Vincent, 2011 ) and combines it with an analytically available likelihood score to perform MCMC directly in data space. Training-time posterior learning. Complementary to test-time guidance, amortized posterior learning trains observation-conditional generators to directly approximate posterior distributions. Neural posterior estimation and related methods learn from simulated parameter-observation pairs, enabling rapid inference for new observations ( Greenberg et al., 2019 ; Radev et al., 2023 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) .
